documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
4 Questions, 60 minutes

**DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN**

- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example, Doe, Jamie / Q1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. Cell phones may not be used during the exam or while the exam papers are present. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Each of the four questions is worth 25 points. The questions are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Good luck!

**Possibly Useful Information**

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Gravitational field at the Earth's surface | $g=9.8\ N/kg$ |
| Newton's gravitational constant | $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ N\cdot m^2/kg^2$ |
| Average Earth-Sun Distance | $1$ Astronomical Unit (A.U.) $=1.5\times10^{11}\ m$ |
| Binomial expansion | $(1+x)^n=1+nx$ for $|x|\ll1$ |

Moment of Inertia about Center of Mass – Uniform Object (will not be provided on the second screening exam)

| Object | Moment of Inertia |
| --- | --- |
| Disk | $\frac12MR^2$ |
| Sphere | $\frac25MR^2$ |
| Rod | $\frac1{12}ML^2$ |

documentNotes.title: Solutions to Problems
documentNotes.statement: Any correct solution should be awarded equivalent points. Suggested partial-credit points are presented in square brackets at the right margin. You may further break down the listed points into one point increments. Where alternate methods are presented, a student should be awarded points from only one method. Students should not be penalized in a subsequent part for using the wrong answer to a previous part. (No double jeopardy.) If it is clear they have done an intermediate step, they should get credit for it even if they have not presented it. For example, in 2.b., if a student wrote down $mvb=mv_pR$, they should get 10 points credit.

problems.statement:
A shell is shot from the edge of a $4.00\ m$ high cliff with initial velocity $v_i$ at an angle of $45.0^\circ$ above the horizontal. It lands $18.0\ m$ from the base of the cliff as shown in the accompanying diagram.

![Shell launched at 45 degrees from a 4.00 m cliff and landing 18.0 m from its base](#p1-fig1-astra-r7-20260925)

parts.label: a
parts.statement: What is the initial speed $v_i$ of the shell?

parts.label: b
parts.statement: A second shell is launched with the same initial velocity. At the top of its trajectory it explodes into two fragments. One fragment of mass $m_1$ has zero speed immediately after the explosion and falls vertically. The other fragment of mass $m_2$ lands $30.0\ m$ from the base of the cliff. Find the ratio $m_1/m_2$.

solution.statement:
**a.** Setting the coordinate origin at the top of the cliff, the horizontal position is given by

$$x=v_{ix}t=(v_i\cos\theta)t=(v_i\cos45.0^\circ)t=\frac{v_it}{\sqrt2}.\tag{1-1}$$

[3] Taking up to be positive, the vertical position is given by

$$y=v_{iy}t-\frac12gt^2=(v_i\sin45.0^\circ)t-\frac12gt^2=\frac{v_it}{\sqrt2}-\frac12gt^2.\tag{1-2}$$

[4] Solving (1-1) for $t$,

$$t=\frac{x\sqrt2}{v_i}.\tag{1-3}$$

[1] Substituting into (1-2),

$$y=\frac{v_i}{\sqrt2}\left(\frac{x\sqrt2}{v_i}\right)-\frac12g\left(\frac{x\sqrt2}{v_i}\right)^2=x-g\frac{x^2}{v_i^2}.$$

[2] Solving for $v_i$, $v_i=\sqrt{gx^2/(x-y)}$. [1] The shell lands at $x=18.0\ m$ and $y=-4.00\ m$, and

$$v_i=\sqrt{\frac{(9.8\ m/s^2)(18.0\ m)^2}{18.0\ m-(-4.0\ m)}}=12.0\ m/s.$$

[2]

**b.** The $y$-component of the velocity is $v_y=v_{iy}-gt=v_i/\sqrt2-gt$. [2] At its highest point, $v_y=0$ and

$$t_h=\frac{v_i}{g\sqrt2}.\tag{1-4}$$

[2] The shell's $x$ position is

$$x=\frac{v_it_h}{\sqrt2}=\frac{v_i}{\sqrt2}\left(\frac{v_i}{g\sqrt2}\right)=\frac{v_i^2}{2g}=\frac{(12.0\ m/s)^2}{2(9.8\ m/s^2)}=7.36\ m.$$

[1]

**METHOD I:** The explosion is an internal force and the motion of the shell's center of mass is unchanged. [2]

*(Note: Since fragment 1 has zero velocity after the explosion, the impulse is totally in the $x$-direction and the fragments land at the same time.)*

Let $x_i$ be the landing position of fragment $m_i$. Fragment 1 falls straight down, so $x_1=7.36\ m$ while $x_2=30.0\ m$. [1] The defining equation of the center of mass of the two fragments is

$$(m_1+m_2)x_{cm}=m_1x_1+m_2x_2.$$

[2]

$$\frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{x_2-x_{cm}}{x_{cm}-x_1}=\frac{30.0\ m-18.0\ m}{18.0\ m-7.4\ m}=1.13.$$

[2]

**METHOD II:** The explosion is an internal force and the total momentum of the shell is unchanged. [1]

*(Note: Since fragment 1 has zero velocity after the explosion, the impulse is totally in the $x$-direction and the $y$-component of momentum is unaffected.)*

For the $x$-component, momentum conservation gives

$$(m_1+m_2)v_{ix}=m_1(0)+m_2v_2=m_2v_2.$$

[1] The velocity of $m_2$ after the explosion is

$$v_2=\frac{(m_1+m_2)v_{ix}}{m_2}=\left(1+\frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)\frac{v_i}{\sqrt2}.$$

[1] The fragment's position after the explosion is

$$x_2=x_h+v_2t_f=x_h+\left(1+\frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)\frac{v_it_f}{\sqrt2}.\tag{1-5}$$

[1] Here $t_f$ is the time it take the fragment to fall from its highest point to the ground. Since the $y$-component of velocity is unchanged by the explosion, the time to fall is the total time (1-3) minus the time to reach the highest point (1-4):

$$t_f=t-t_h=\frac{x\sqrt2}{v_i}-\frac{v_i}{g\sqrt2}=\frac{(18.0\ m)\sqrt2}{12.0\ m/s}-\frac{12.0\ m/s}{(9.8\ m/s^2)\sqrt2}=1.255\ s.$$

[2]

*(The time can also be obtained by first finding the $y$-displacement at the highest point and then finding the time to fall from that point to the ground. Using either method a time of $1.26\ s$ should get 2 points credit.)*

Solving (1-5) for the mass ratio,

$$\frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{(x_2-x_h)\sqrt2}{v_it_f}-1=\frac{(30.0\ m-7.36\ m)\sqrt2}{(12.0\ m/s)(1.255\ s)}-1=1.13.$$

[1]

problems.title: “Hit the planet, win a prize.”
problems.statement:
A space probe is sent toward a distant planet which has mass $M$ and radius $R$. When the probe is very, very far from the planet, the probe has speed $v$ and is headed in a direction such that, if undeflected, it would pass a distance $b>R$ from the planet's center. See the accompanying diagram.

![Incoming probe with speed v and impact parameter b relative to a planet of mass M and radius R](#p2-fig1-astra-r7-20260925)

parts.label: a
parts.statement: Assuming that the probe hits the planet, what is the probe's speed just before it hits?

parts.label: b
parts.statement: What is the maximum initial speed the probe can have and still hit the planet?

solution.statement:
**a.** Using energy conservation, the total mechanical energy when the probe is an infinite distance from the planet equals the total mechanical energy just before the probe hits:

$$K_\infty+U_\infty=K_p+U_p.$$

[2] Setting $U_\infty=0$, [1] we have $U_p=-GMm/R$, [2] where $m$ is the mass of the probe. The probe's kinetic energy is $K_\infty=\frac12mv^2$ and $K_p=\frac12mv_p^2$, [2] where $v_p$ is the probe's speed just before it hits the surface. Combining,

$$\frac12mv^2=\frac12mv_p^2-\frac{GMm}{R}.\tag{2-1}$$

[1] Solving for $v_p$, we have $v_p=\sqrt{v^2+2GM/R}$. [2]

**b.** A central force, such as the universal gravitational force, causes no torque. Therefore angular momentum is conserved: $L_\infty=L_p$. [2] Angular momentum is given by

$$\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p=\vec r\times m\vec v.\tag{2-2}$$

[2] Conservation gives $\vec r_\infty\times m\vec v=\vec r_p\times m\vec v_p$. [1] When the probe is very far away,

$$|\vec r_\infty\times m\vec v|=mvr_\infty\sin\theta=mvb.\tag{2-3}$$

[2] When the probe has the largest speed it can have and still hit the planet, it will come in tangential to the surface, or perpendicular to the radius.

$$|\vec r_p\times m\vec v_p|=mv_pR.\tag{2-4}$$

[2] Combining (2-2), (2-3), and (2-4), $mvb=mv_pR$. [1] Solving for $v_p$,

$$v_p=v\frac bR.\tag{2-5}$$

[1] Substituting (2-5) into (2-1),

$$\frac12mv^2=\frac12m\left(v\frac bR\right)^2-\frac{GMm}{R}.$$

[2]

$$v^2\left[\left(\frac bR\right)^2-1\right]=\frac{2GM}{R},$$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R[(b/R)^2-1]}}=\sqrt{\frac{2GMR}{b^2-R^2}}.$$

[2]

figures.alt: Incoming probe with speed v and impact parameter b relative to a planet of mass M and radius R

problems.statement:
![Compressed spring and block on a rough surface with initial displacement A0](#p3-fig1-astra-r7-20260925)

A mass $M$ with weight $Mg=10.00\ N$ is placed at the end of a massless spring with spring constant $100.0\ N/m$ as shown in the above diagram. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between the mass and the rough horizontal surface are $0.400$ and $0.200$, respectively. The spring is compressed a distance $A_0=0.180\ m$ from its equilibrium position and released from rest. Find the total distance the mass travels and where it comes to rest with respect to the equilibrium position.

solution.statement:
In order for the mass to continue to oscillate back and forth, the spring force at maximum extension must exceed the maximum force of static friction. Letting $A_i$ equal the maximum displacement after the $i$th half cycle.

The mass stops oscillating when $F|_{x=A_i}<f_{s,max}$. [2] The spring force has magnitude $F=kx$. [1] The maximum force of static friction is $f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=\mu_sMg$. [2] The oscillation stops if $kA_i<\mu_sMg$. [1] Or numerically,

$$A_i<\frac{\mu_sMg}{k}=\frac{(0.400)(10.00\ N)}{100.0\ N/m}=0.0400\ m.\tag{3-1}$$

[1] Applying the work energy theorem to a single half oscillation,

$$W_{nc}+K_i+U_i=K_{i+1}+U_{i+1},\tag{3-2}$$

[2] where $W_{nc}$ is the work done by non-conservative forces, friction in this case. At the extreme displacements $A_i$ and $A_{i+1}$, the kinetic energy is zero: at $x=A_i$ and $x=A_{i+1}$, $K_i=0$ and $K_{i+1}=0$. [1]

The spring potential energy at $A_i$ and $A_{i+1}$ is $U_i=\frac12kA_i^2$ and $U_{i+1}=\frac12kA_{i+1}^2$. [1] The work done by kinetic friction is $W_{nc}=-f_kd=-\mu_kMgd$, [2] where $d$ is the total distance traveled, or $d=A_i+A_{i+1}$. [1]

$$W_{nc}=-\mu_kMg(A_i+A_{i+1}).$$

[1] Substituting into (3-2),

$$-\mu_kMg(A_i+A_{i+1})+\frac12kA_i^2=\frac12kA_{i+1}^2.$$

[1]

$$\mu_kMg(A_i+A_{i+1})=\frac12k(A_i^2-A_{i+1}^2)=\frac12k(A_i+A_{i+1})(A_i-A_{i+1}).$$

Dividing by $(A_i+A_{i+1})$, $\mu_kMg=\frac12k(A_i-A_{i+1})$. Solving for $A_{i+1}$,

$$A_{i+1}=A_i-\frac{2\mu_kMg}{k}.$$

[2] Numerically,

$$A_{i+1}=A_i-\frac{2(0.200)(10.00\ N)}{100.0\ N/m}=A_i-0.0400\ m.$$

Therefore each half cycle the amplitude decreases by $0.040\ m=4.0\ cm$. [1]

Successive amplitudes (starting with the initial displacement) are $0.180\ m$, $0.140\ m$, $0.100\ m$, $0.060\ m$, $0.020\ m$. [2] At $0.020\ m$ the amplitude satisfies condition (3-1) and the mass remains at rest. Since $A_0$ is to the left of the equilibrium position and they alternate, the stopping point is $0.020\ m$ to the left of the equilibrium position. [2]

The total distance traveled is $D=A_0+2A_1+2A_2+2A_3+A_4$.

$$D=(0.180\ m)+2(0.140\ m)+2(0.100\ m)+2(0.060\ m)+(0.020\ m)=0.800\ m.$$

[2]

figures.alt: Compressed spring and block on a rough surface with initial displacement A0

answer.value: 0.800 m total distance; stops 0.020 m to the left of the equilibrium position.

problems.statement:
![Top and side views of a disk pulled by a cord tangent to its rim](#p4-fig1-astra-r7-20260925)

A thin disk of mass $M$, radius $R$, and height $H$ is initially at rest on a flat horizontal table as shown in top and side views above. There is no friction between the disk and the table. A long massless cord is wrapped around the disk and pulled with constant force $F$ parallel to the table.

parts.label: a
parts.statement: Find the ratio of rotational to translational kinetic energy.

parts.label: b
parts.statement: What is the total work done by the force $F$ during the disk's first revolution?

solution.statement:
**a.** The translational kinetic energy is $K_t=\frac12Mv^2$ or $K_t=W_F=Fd$, [2] where $v$ is the time-dependent translational speed. From Newton's Second Law with $F$ the only force acting, the acceleration of the center of mass is given by $a=F/M$. [1] Starting from rest, $v=at=Ft/M$ or $d=\frac12at^2=Ft^2/(2M)$. [2] By either method, the translational kinetic energy is

$$K_t=\frac12M\left(\frac{Ft}{M}\right)^2=\frac{F^2t^2}{2M}\quad\text{or}\quad K_t=F\left(\frac{Ft^2}{2M}\right)=\frac{F^2t^2}{2M}.\tag{4-1}$$

[1] The rotational kinetic energy is $K_r=\frac12I\omega^2$ or $K_r=\tau\theta$, [2] where $\omega$ is the time-dependent rotational speed, $\theta$ is the angular displacement, $\tau$ is the torque, and $I$ the disk's rotational inertia about its center of mass: $I=\frac12MR^2$. [1] The torque about the center of mass is $|\vec\tau|=|\vec R\times\vec F|=RF$. [1] From Newton's Second Law for rotational motion the angular acceleration about the center of mass is given by

$$\alpha=\frac\tau I=\frac{RF}{\frac12MR^2}=\frac{2F}{MR}.\tag{4-2}$$

[1] Starting from rest, $\omega=\alpha t=2Ft/(MR)$ or $\theta=\frac12\alpha t^2=Ft^2/(MR)$. [2] By either method, the rotational kinetic energy is

$$K_r=\frac12\left(\frac12MR^2\right)\left(\frac{2Ft}{MR}\right)^2=\frac{F^2t^2}{M}\quad\text{or}\quad K_r=(RF)\frac{Ft^2}{MR}=\frac{F^2t^2}{M}.\tag{4-3}$$

[1] Dividing (4-3) by (4-1),

$$\frac{K_r}{K_t}=\frac{F^2t^2/M}{F^2t^2/(2M)}=2.$$

[1]

*Note:*

$$\frac{K_r}{K_t}=\frac{\frac12I\omega^2}{\frac12Mv^2}=\frac{(\frac12MR^2)\omega^2}{Mv^2}=\frac12\left(\frac{\omega R}{v}\right)^2.$$

*This is not rolling without slipping and $v\ne\omega R$. The answer $\frac12$ is only worth 4 points.*

**b.** The net work done by the force is equal to the change in kinetic energy: $W=\Delta K_t+\Delta K_r$. [2] Since the disk starts at rest both initial kinetic energies are zero and

$$W=K_t+K_r=\frac{F^2t^2}{2M}+\frac{F^2t^2}{M}=\frac{3F^2t^2}{2M},\tag{4-4}$$

[3] where $t$ is the time it takes to make the first rotation. With uniform angular acceleration and starting from rest,

$$\theta=\frac12\alpha t^2.\tag{4-5}$$

[1] From (4-2), $\alpha=2F/(MR)$, [1] and for a single rotation $\theta=2\pi$. [1] Solving (4-5) for $t^2$,

$$t^2=\frac{2\theta}{\alpha}=\frac{2(2\pi)}{2F/(MR)}=\frac{2\pi MR}{F}.$$

[1] Substituting into (4-4),

$$W=\frac{3F^2t^2}{2M}=\frac{3F^2}{2M}\left(\frac{2\pi MR}{F}\right)=3\pi FR.$$

[1]
